title: Is anybody really using Claude Fable 5?
summary: How Anthropic ran through its goodwill faster than it takes Fable 5 to burn $1,000 in tokens, and why almost nobody is using it for work.
articleHtml:
How Anthropic ran through its goodwill faster than it takes Fable 5 to burn $1,000 in tokens, and why almost nobody is using it for work.

Disclaimer: No AI was used in the writing, reviewing, or editing of this article.

Fable 5. Anthropic’s “Mythos-class” Artificial Intelligence model which they have bubble-wrapped just enough to permit us less civilized chimps to touch. “Mythos-class”, I say, but not actually “Mythos”, because that model is too dangerous for the average you-and-me — we could hurt ourselves and those around us. It is for our own good, of course, in the same way that I don’t let my young kids play with knives. We thank His Grace, King Dario, the First of His Name, Father of the Claudes, Protector of the Neural Nets.

“Back in my day…”, said the old man

If I sound bitter, it’s because I am. I’ve been working in AI for a long time — long before the term “Prompt Engineering” existed — back when, if you did something significant in the field, the obvious thing to do was to publish everything — the code, the paper, the metrics. We didn’t just stand on the shoulders of giants, we got together to make human-pyramids.

The reason we moved away from this paradigm, the reason so much of AI became proprietary and closed-source, was because, post ChatGPT, the tremendous commercial benefits of AI became apparent to the investor-class. See investors don’t invest if what they are investing in can be “stolen” by others — obviously. From then on, the deal was that the so-called “frontier-labs” — then the OpenAIs and DeepMinds of the world — would continue carrying our torch, using their disgusting amounts of funding to push R&D and make it accessible to the rest of us, the peasants, at an affordable cost. In return, we would build, build, build like never before — at home, at work, on vacation, everywhere — and make their investors happy with the increasing subscription numbers.

The Rise of Anthropic

Anthropic, specifically, made its name as the company for the little-guy — the pro-developer and pro-safety alternative to OpenAI which promised both more “Open” and more “AI”. Claude Code was a masterstroke, and was adopted by the hackers and the nerds en-masse almost overnight. Anthropic used this rapid adoption and fervor to become favourable to enterprise customers (think big business behemoths, like Warlmart, TD Bank, PwC, or the Government). The pitch was simple — your tech-people already use Claude Code at home, why not wrap it in a security blanket and use it at work to increase every engineer’s efficiency? The pitch worked fantastically. Within a matter of months, I saw “ChatGPT” fade away from business lexicon whilst everyone in the industry had a buddy named “Claude”.

When, in early 2026, Anthropic refused to bend the knee to part-time Secretary of Defence, full-time war enthusiast, and the greatest strategist the world has ever known — Pete “Genghis” Hegseth — it endeared them to the average person even more. Not allowing their models to be used for autonomous killing and surveillance of US civilians would seem like a pretty low bar, and yet, Anthropic ended up being the standard bearer of AI’s resistance to authoritarianism - OpenAI, Google, SpacexAI , Microsoft — all seem to have silently agreed to DoD’s terms. I remember having conversations with multiple people in my circle who claimed to have cancelled their ChatGPT subscriptions in the following weeks. Anthropic was on an historic rise, and the numbers proved it.

The Fall from Grace

That brings me back to Mythos and Fable. With the announcement of Mythos, Anthropic decided to renege on their unspoken promise — they screwed-over the little guy who made them mainstream by allowing only a select few companies access to, what they claimed was, the unprecedented intelligence of Mythos. The name of the initiative? Project Glasswing — which I originally thought would make a good James Bond movie, but now think is more appropriate for the next Johnny English. This, obviously, did not go down well with the public — me included. Nobody likes being told that they cannot have a new toy because they cannot be trusted with it.

A few weeks later, when they released the much softened version of Mythos called Fable 5, they exceeded their own silliness by putting unfathomably ridiculous guardrails and rules around it. The most notables ones were:

  1. The 30-day data retention policy, stating that Anthropic would store all data sent to Fable 5 for 30-days regardless of who it came from. This essentially ensured that Enterprise customers, for whom data is a competitive advantage, wouldn’t touch it with a 10ft pole. At my work, for example, I have access to every non-Chinese model under the sun except, you guessed it, Fable 5.
  2. Silent-degradation, where Fable 5 silently delegates its tasks to Opus if it deems the request to be too dangerous (or something — nobody really knows), ensured that one could never trust its outputs. Imagine hiring a professional contractor to paint your house, who then delegates the task to a neighborhood teenager without asking you!
  3. Removing Fable 5 from their lowest-tier paid plans. This, more than anything else, was a kick in the teeth of their largest and most staunch user-base — the average coder just trying to make something cool.
  4. The extremely hard, extremely silly refusals. Asking anything even remotely science-y would be met with a refusal. On Day 1 of Fable 5’s rollout, before it was temporarily banned, I tested this with a colleague by asking it “What is Cancer?”. It politely told me sit down and shut up.

But that was not enough. Since Fable 5’s botched re-rollout, Anthropic has now emerged as the singular, most prominent opposing force against open-weight models — the ones that offer consumers lower cost, reliable alternatives. Kind Dario, ever-caring, believes that powerful open weight-models in the hands of every developer is akin to assault rifles in the hands of monkeys — there is very little chance of it not being a disaster. We are to believe that his opposition is rooted entirely in public good and national security, of course, and not at all in the fact that cheaper alternatives create market pressure for Anthropic.

Imagine how unpopular your position must be when every major tech company and developer is against it.

Honestly, I have rarely seen so much goodwill lost so quickly. It took Meta years to accomplish the level of public distrust that Anthropic managed to acquire in 60 days starting June 2026. It’s quite commendable in its own way.

So, the question is, if not enterprise users, not hackers, and not hobbyists — who is using Fable 5?

The only people I see using Fable 5 regularly are YouTubers, Podcasters, and some Redditors— and for the same reason — to tell the rest of us what we are missing out on. What percentage of Claude’s users subscribe to a paid plan? What percentage of those subscriptions are for the Max plan? What percentage of API-based users are also non-Enterprise users?

Let’s do some quick, dirty, completely unreliable math.

First, assumptions:

  • Let’s say that daily Claude users are split evenly into paid and free
  • It is likely that the vast majority of API-based users overlap with Enterprise users, based on the assumption that the average hobbyist or start-up cannot afford to pay by token.
  • I would also argue that the majority of paid users are hobbyists — hackers, part-time developers, tinkerers, learners — and are on the basic paid plan, not Max.

Now, let’s math:

So who is really using Fable 5? According to my back-of-the-envelope calculation, about 7% of total Claude users.

Considering how expensive a model is to develop, then train, then post-train, then productize, then serve — this could not have been the plan. But, who am I to question His Grace, King Dario, the First of His Name, Father of the Claudes, Protector of the Neural Nets.
